thread.title: Stocks Tumble As Apple Cripples Global Tech Stocks | Investor's Business Daily

author: ALAN R. ELLIOTT
title: Stocks Tumble As Apple Cripples Global Tech Stocks | Investor's Business Daily
text:
Bad news from Apple ( AAPL ) sent stocks sprawling at the starting bell Thursday, as a tech stock led sell-off drove the Dow Jones industrial average down more than 450 points in early trade.
X A pullback in Apple's outlook was the hub of global investor attention early Thursday as shares leaned toward their worst loss in a half decade. The lack of any progress among U.S. legislators in a White House meeting Wednesday sent the broadening shutdown of federal offices into its 12th day. Better-than-expected jobs data were a positive note in early trade, ahead of the December payrolls report due Friday.
Chip stocks were among the early casualties as Apple suppliers were slammed in early trade. Chipmakers ST Microelectronics ( STM ) and Cirrus Logic ( CRUS ) posted some of the deepest declines. On the IBD 50 list , chipmakers Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Intel ( INTC ) lodged heavy losses. On the upside, biotech Celgene ( CELG ) rocketed on news of a takeover by Bristol-Myers Squibb ( BMY ), and Gilead Sciences ( GILD ) jumped on an analyst upgrade.
The Dow Jones industrial average traded down 2%. The Dow's tech stocks performed worst, with Apple and Intel leading the declines.
The Nasdaq Composite dug into a 2.2% loss. Apple and Skyworks Solutions ( SWKS ) were near the head of the slide. American Airlines Group ( AAL ) was the Nasdaq 100's top decliner. Airlines stocks plummeted after Delta Air Lines ( DAL ) reported its Q4 operating guidance, and an American jet was forced to make an emergency landing in Phoenix due to smoke in the cabin.
The S&P 500 dived 1.7%. Bristol-Myers notched the deepest decline among S&P 500 names, followed by American Airlines.

Please contact customer service CLOSE Stock Market: Still In A Correction On Wednesday, heavy opening losses on the Dow Jones industrial average, S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite gave way to modest gains by the close. Such late-day strength is generally considered to be bullish. But the unpredictable current stock market is still in a correction , and the volatility is a strong reminder that hands-off observation is, for now, the best strategy.
If the rally attempt begun last week posts a follow-through day , the market's status will shift from "market in correction" to "confirmed uptrend." That change would flash the green light for investors to begin jumping into stocks breaking out from valid bases.
Apple Dives — Is It Another Flash Crash? Apple stock dived nearly 9%, potentially moving toward their worst loss since January 2014. (Apple shares had dived 13% in early trade during its "flash crash" on August 24, 105, but the stock recovered to a loss of only 2.5%.)
A letter to shareholders from Chief Executive Tim Cook warned that Apple's December-quarter revenue would be more than $7 billion below analyst forecasts of $91.49 billion. Cook cited "economic deceleration, particularly in Greater China," for the reduced outlook.
Apple shares had been scooping a neat base, with 10-week support. Premarket action, though, pointed to an open sharply below the 10-week line. Not all premarket moves carry over into regular trade.
China Stock Market Dips; London Turns Positive Stock markets in China posted modest losses Thursday, with Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index ending 0.3% lower and the Shanghai Composite a fraction below its starting point. Early automated trading briefly upended currency markets, sending the yen soaring against the U.S. dollar, and the Australian dollar to a 10-year low.
In Japan, the Tokyo Stock Exchange remained closed on holiday. Korea's KOSPI benchmark dived 0.8%.
Stocks in Europe came off their lows and turned mixed in afternoon trade, although Apple's news continued to draw down technology stocks. Frankfurt's DAX eased to a 0.9% decline. The CAC-40 in Paris narrowed to an 0.8% loss, while London's FTSE 100 reversed early losses and climbed into narrow gains.
Stocks: Celgene Surges; American, Delta Air Dive Celgene spiked 28% on news that Bristol-Myers Squibb would acquire the New Jersey-based biotech in a cash-and-stock deal valued at $74 billion . Celgene shares had dropped 55% over the past 14 months. Bristol-Myers stock swooned 12% in opening trade.
Another biotech, Gilead Sciences, jumped more than 4% in early action. Oppenheimer upgraded the stock to outperform, from perform. Gilead has rebounded in the past three sessions, after diving below its 200-day moving average on Dec. 23.
American Airlines collapsed 11%, Delta Air dropped more than 9%, despite Delta raising its fourth-quarter earnings guidance. The airline said unit revenues, an important passenger metric, likely rose 3%, below prior guidance for a 3.5% gain. An American jet bound for New York out of Los Angeles diverted to Phoenix, after a "sudden burst of smoke" in the aircraft's cabin.
December Jobs Data Positive; Layoffs Accelerate In Q4 Markets will be keenly focused on the pending December payrolls report, due out Friday despite the widening shutdown of federal offices in Washington. Two precursors to that report came out early Thursday.
U.S. employers announced 17% fewer layoffs in December than in November, according to the monthly Job Cuts Report from Challenger, Gray & Christmas. That left the tally for 2018 about 29% higher than in 2017, with job cuts accelerating to 43% in the fourth quarter.
The National Employment Report from ADP estimated U.S. non-farm employers added 271,000 workers in December. That was more than 70% higher than November's new hires, and far above economist estimates for 175,000 new workers. Some 83% of the hiring was done by service-sector employers. On the goods-producing side, 37,000 of the new jobs were in construction and 12,000 in manufacturing, while mining and resources industries gave up 2,000 workers.
First-time unemployment claims came in higher than expected, at 231,000 new applications for the week ended Dec. 29, according to the Labor Department. Consensus estimates had called for 217,000 applications, essentially the same as the prior week. Some 800,000 federal workers are currently idled, with many of those being advised to file unemployment claims.
